column693: A lowland species found mainly below 200 m elevation, which is certainly true of known Australian populations, but it has been recorded from 0--1500 m elevation across its range. Typically found on sandy to clay soils along watercourses, along the margins of swamps and in seasonally wet savannahs in fully exposed to moderately shaded situations. It typically favours drier situations than N. rowaniae and N. tenax where the species co-occur, whereas in various parts of Southeast Asia it has been documented growing in permanent bodies of shallow water. High elevation populations are more typically observed in large mountain complexes or upland plateaus as a result of the Massenerhebung (mountain mass) effect, which sees warmer conditions manifested at higher elevations (A. column696: Clearance of Nitraria billardierei for control of feral species is often a controversial subject. It has been allowed in some parts of South Australia under State legislation but permission still needs to be sought from the Native Vegetation Council. Leaves and inflorescences often have gall-like infestations and these may well prove of interest since gall-forming armoured scale insects (Diaspidiotus species) have been documented on Nitraria species elsewhere (E.M. Danzig, J. Zoosyst. Rossica 8: 287--289 (1999). Similarly, the sphecid wasps Solierella nitraria Pulawski and Cerceris nitrariae Morice (R.M. Bohart & A.S. Menke, Sphecid wasps of the world: a generic revision (1976)) described from Egypt and Morocco respectively, were named for their association with Nitraria species and it would be interesting to see whether these same associations occur in Australian populations. The fruits of Nitraria billardierei are edible and particularly attractive to emus, and possibly to rock-parrots (S.A. White, Emu 16: 1--15 (1916)), but are also taken by kangaroos, sheep, rabbits, lizards and decorator ants; germination was found to be enhanced after passage through an emu (J.C. Noble, J. Ecol. 63: 979--984 (1975)). N. billardierei fruits have also been recorded as part of the diet of Australian Aborigines (B. Gott, Telopea 12: 215--226 (2008)) and have been eaten without any ill effects by the author. They have potential for development as a native food, although a little salty. Possibly not distinct from the Russian species Nitraria schoberi. While there is a documented chromosome number difference (2n = 24 for N. schoberi and 2n = 48 for N. billardierei), morphological differences, including spininess and leaf and floral characteristics, have not been investigated fully. Morphological differences, including habit and size of the stones, were documented by Noble & Whalley (1978a) between the populations of Nitraria billardierei occurring along the Indian Ocean and those which occur along the Southern Ocean. Again, a molecular study across the range of the species could prove useful, particularly given the expanding distribution in inland areas.

Instead, the outer reticulately-marked surface expanded, apparently trapping a great deal of air between it and the embryo. Seeds also yield a dye called “Turkey Red” used for colouring tarbooshes (Mabberley 1987: 437) and for dyeing carpets in Turkey and Iran (Emboden 1972) but other references within dyeing books also attribute the dye known by this name to Madder (Rubia tinctorum). The colour of the dye extracted from the seeds depends on whether the extraction is done in water (yellow fluorescent) or alcohol (red). Peganum harmala plants have an unpleasant smell and are possibly poisonous to livestock. The alkaloids contained within the roots and seeds possibly account for this, as they may also account for a number of reputed medicinal properties ranging from emetic to antispasmodic, narcotic, stimulant and antihelminthic (Ghafoor 1977: 9). Emboden (1972) also refers to the aphrodisiac, narcotic and hallucinogenic properties of Peganum harmala. The properties of Peganum harmala are also provided by Parsons & Cuthbertson (2001: 637--639).

Within populations, the size of the plants can vary considerably and extremely small plants may produce a frond a few centimetres long. In such small plants the fertile sporophore is simple, with the sporangia in 2 rows; however, there are usually paired sporangia at the base of the sporophore. Thus, although they usually have entire or slightly irregular margins, these are occasionally prominently crenulate and often have 1 medial or a number of incisions dissecting the pinnae. This latter situation appears to correlate with very robust plants. Very rarely up to 3 fertile sporophores may arise on a frond, each with its own stipe. I have also observed the occasional plant of B. australe to produce a second fertile sporophore.

The bee probes the calli and labellum sac for about 30 seconds before backing out, often receiving the orchid’s pollinarium on the thorax. The fragrant flowers last less than day, opening early in morning and often finishing by midday. Sections of flowers on the racemes open simultaneously in spasms and generally all the plants in an area flower at same time, known as synchronous flowering or massed gregarious flowering. column692: The flowers open fully during day and partially close at night with the tepals incurving over the column and labellum. The flowers last 1--3 days and have a fruity fragrance that specifically attracts male fruit flies of the genus Bactrocera (order Diptera, family Tephrotidae); 2 common native species are B. jarvisi and B. tryoni. These male fruit flies do not attempt to mate with the flowers but instead feed in the flower and take in chemical components of the floral fragrance which are vital for specific aspects of the insect’s sex life and reproduction (Tan & Nishida 2007). The flies visit the flowers in the morning and probe the sepals and petals, eventually feeding on the labellum which tips when the point of balance is passed trapping the insect against the column. While attempting to retreat the fly becomes stuck firmly in the viscidium, sometimes for more than 30 minutes, all the while struggling until eventually it frees itself with the pollinarium attached to its back. Pollination occurs when the insect visits another flower. See also Teck et al. (2011). Sometimes the insect perishes after becoming trapped in the flower (Smythe 1969, personal observations).

column692: The relatively large flowers release a strong, unusual scent that smells like semen or fish meal. Nectar, exuded in large droplets, coalesces in the labellum groove and also flows into small pouches formed by the lateral sepals. The scent is very noticeable on warm days and attracts blowflies of genus Calliphora (family Calliphoridae), particularly C. tibialis, which actively work the flowers and feed on the nectar. The labellum tip is at first outwards as the fly feeds, but as the fly moves forwards the labellum eventually tips inwards and traps fly between the column and labellum. The fly buzzes furiously while trapped, eventually picking up pollinarium on its thorax. Pollen is transferred to the broad, sticky stigma of another flower on a subsequent visit. For details of pollination see Jones (1985).
